props.alt: Tranquil brick courtyard garden with reflection basin, gravel path and sliding oak glass doors

props.text: Inward gardens that anchor daily domestic rhythm.
Rather than pushing outdoor space to a residual lawn, our residential commissions wrap rooms around a sheltered court that moderates wind, rain and seasonal sun.
Daylight enters living and kitchen spaces from both the street edge and the planted central court.
Deep brick reveals and custom pivot doors turn weather transitions into calm outdoor rooms.
Perimeter garden walls create quiet dining terraces even within compact city neighborhoods.

props.alt: Converted brick warehouse interior with retained historical timber roof trusses and limewashed masonry

props.text: New civic and studio life inside retained industrial shells.
Existing buildings hold irreplaceable embodied carbon, patina and spatial generosity. We audit structural capacity first and intervene with surgical restraint.
Retaining foundation slabs, load-bearing masonry and heavy timber frames cuts structural carbon by up to 65%.
Concealed steel strongbacks and breathable wood-fiber insulation modernize envelopes without erasing patina.
Inserted roof monitors and timber slat baffles turn echoey warehouses into warm working halls.

props.alt: Neighborhood timber-and-brick cultural pavilion with clerestory north light and oak benches

props.text: Durable neighborhood rooms built for fifty-year stewardship.
We partner with community land trusts, libraries and arts foundations to design welcoming public buildings with low operating costs and self-finishing materials.
Clear public thresholds invite neighbors inside while keeping staff sightlines unobstructed.
Stack-effect operable transoms and deep overhangs reduce mechanical cooling demand year-round.
Unpainted lime plaster, oiled oak and quarry tile age gracefully under heavy daily footfall.

props.alt: Full-scale architectural mockups of Roman clay brick, lime mortar, white oak joinery and brass hardware

props.text: Full-scale joinery mockups and regional supply chains.
Every commission is developed alongside regional brick kilns, FSC sawmills and metal fabricators through physical 1:1 corner and window assemblies.
Traditional hydraulic lime mortars allow historic and new masonry to dry naturally without spalling.
Pegged oak and Douglas fir joinery keeps structural logic legible and simplifies future disassembly.
Bricks, basalts and structural softwoods are sourced within 250 miles of each building site.
Details designed to weather rather than wear out.

props.alt: Pale-brick courtyard residence with oak-framed openings and planted gravel garden in morning light

props.text: “Rather than looking across an exposed pasture, we brought the garden to the center of the plan.”

On a windy Willamette Valley ridge, rural residences often lose usable outdoor seasons for six months of the year. By enclosing a thirty-two-by-thirty-eight-foot courtyard inside continuous double-wythe brick walls, every room opens to calm air, filtered maple shade and borrowed daylight.

A continuous glazed white-oak cloister links the family kitchen, reading library and grandparents’ sleeping wing. On mild mornings, ten-foot pivot doors swing open so the indoor oak dining table and the crushed limestone court operate as one room.
Balancing north courtyard glazing with deep-set south apertures eliminates daytime glare and electric lighting needs.
The guest and grandparent wing sits across the planted court from the kitchen, connected by a sheltered colonnade.
Unsealed interior clay brick wythes store winter low-angle sun and release gentle radiant warmth after dusk.

props.text: From a focused feasibility study to site supervision.
We sequence work in five clear phases so owners can test zoning limits, daylight options and contractor pricing before full technical documentation.
Start small. Commit only after clarity.
Clients regularly hire us for a standalone Phase I study during property due diligence before proceeding into full architectural design.
Phase I Feasibility Dossiers begin at $7,500 for existing townhouses and $9,500 for new residential sites.
Phase I · Pre-Design & Fabric Feasibility (4–6 Weeks)
Site walks, laser scanning of existing structures, zoning and shoreline overlay analysis, structural retention audits, and target cost benchmarking.
Output: Survey dossier, two massing studies, and fixed construction cost benchmark.
Phase II · Schematic Design & 1:20 Models (6–8 Weeks)
Establish room proportions, courtyard shelter, solar aperture studies and primary timber or masonry structural bays tested through physical basswood models.
Output: Schematic plans & sections, 1:20 model, and builder pre-construction estimate.
Phase III · Design Development & Mockups (8–10 Weeks)
Structural, MEP and landscape integration alongside full-scale custom cabinet, stair joinery, brick bond and window reveal mockups.
Output: Coordinated permit-ready drawings, window schedule, and physical sample box.
Phase IV · Technical Construction Documents (10–12 Weeks)
Detailed drawings and CSI specification manuals governing waterproofing, acoustic assemblies, thermal breaks and concealed seismic hardware.
Output: Stamped municipal permit set and competitive/negotiated contractor pricing.
Weekly site visits reviewing shop drawings, mortar sample panels and millwork fit, culminating in commissioning and a twelve-month seasonal walk.
Output: Field reports, mockup sign-offs, and owner building stewardship manual.

items.q: Can we hire Common Ground for a Phase I Feasibility Study before purchasing a property or warehouse?

items.a: We recommend selecting a craft-aligned general contractor on a negotiated pre-construction basis at the end of Schematic Design (Phase II). Early builder input on local masonry, timber sourcing and site logistics prevents budget surprises later.
items.q: When do you bring a general contractor into the process?

items.a: Yes. Built-in white-oak cabinetry, library shelving, lighting and courtyard threshold gardens are integral to our architectural scope, and we collaborate closely with regional landscape ecologists.
